title: Substance and appearance (ST III.75)
hookLine: Thomas explains transubstantiation: the substance changes while appearances remain
carry: what it is, not how it looks

lines: EVERYTHING ABOUT HOW HE LOOKS CHANGED.
cards: At a family reunion, an old woman squints across the yard at a tall man with a gray beard and a cane. She doesn't recognize him. His hair is gone, he's far heavier than the skinny kid she used to babysit.
Then he laughs, and she says his name. Everything about how he looks has changed. Who he is hasn't.
Hold on to that, because Thomas Aquinas is about to turn it inside out. Today, the word he builds his account of the Eucharist on: substance.

teach.b: Thomas uses two words from philosophy. Substance is what a thing is. Accidents are the features it has: color, size, taste, weight, place.
Usually the accidents change and the substance stays, like the man at the reunion. At Mass, Thomas says, it happens the other way around.
At the Last Supper Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." The Catholic Church takes those words literally.

teach.h: THE SUBSTANCE CHANGES, THE LOOK REMAINS.
teach.b: The whole substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body, and the wine into his blood, while the accidents remain: the color, taste and weight of bread and wine.

The Church names this transubstantiation, first met on day one hundred fourteen: a change of substance. Thomas is careful about what it isn't. Christ's body doesn't travel down from heaven and push the bread aside.
Nothing moves. It's a change in what is there, not where something goes. Why keep the look and taste of bread?
People don't eat human flesh, and it would horrify them; so the gift comes as ordinary food. And it leaves room for faith. Are the senses fooled, then?

The senses judge appearances, and the appearances really are there. It's the mind, by faith, that knows what is underneath. In John, Jesus says: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed."
Christians understand this differently. Orthodox Christians also speak of a real change, without Thomas's terms; some Protestant churches understand the bread as a sign or memorial.
Thomas's word asks you to look past how something looks to what it is.

how: Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle where the Eucharist is reserved, receive Communion at Mass, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, where people sit or kneel in prayer before the host.

o: what a thing is, beneath how it looks
the stuff a thing is physically made of
the most important point of an argument

games.q: substance and appearance — tap the pairs.

s: for Thomas, Christ's body travels down from heaven to the altar
nothing moves, he says. it's a change in what is there, not where something goes.
Thomas says the senses are fooled at Mass
the senses judge appearances, and those really remain. faith knows the substance.
Thomas gives reasons why the look and taste of bread remain
people don't eat human flesh, so the gift comes as ordinary food, and it leaves room for faith.

games.q: you're Thomas. a student says: if this is Christ's body, why does it still taste like bread? are my senses lying? what do you answer?
o: no: your senses judge appearances, which remain; faith knows the substance.
the body has moved in and pushed the bread aside.
games.why: Thomas says the senses aren't deceived, since the appearances are really there. the change is in substance, and nothing moves.

practice: Catholic churches keep the Eucharist in a tabernacle, and some leave their doors open; if you can stop in, sit near it for a while without saying much.
If you can't, and you pray, turn your attention toward the nearest tabernacle you know. If you don't pray, look at one ordinary thing near you and ask what it is, beneath how it looks.

wordCard.voice: Substance. What a thing is, beneath the features you can see and touch. For Thomas, at Mass the substance changes while the appearances remain. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a change of substance, the Church's word for the change at Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: what it is, not how it looks. People, too, are more than a glance can catch. Until tomorrow.
